note_tweet.text:
Agent platform 2027

Agents as actors

The status quo for most scalable agent workloads is to deploy agents using some form of Temporal. I think this will shift toward actors that allow each agent harness to have a fully independent runtime. The actor model provides runtime isolation, which is necessary for self-improving harnesses, where self-improving refers to an agent being able to write its own extensions or hooks on the fly. Actors help because they allow different implementations of the agent loop to run safely on the same platform backend, even within a single tenant.

The platform should support a variety of agent configurations, separating the definition of an agent from its instances and sessions. Some users may want a mega-agent, but others may prefer bespoke agent definitions. Most notably, Anthropic argues for one mega-agent, but its revealed preference in Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem (https://t.co/WlH1HDPRAm) suggests something different: each agent had access to only a shell and a file editor. It's unclear to me whether, even if Opus can distinguish the right tools, the researchers would have wanted agents loaded with Gmail, Google Drive, and internet search MCPs when commanding this swarm. Therefore, even within companies advocating for one mega-agent, my observation is that their revealed preference is closer to a code-defined "Grokbot" model.

Relevant: Cloudflare DO, Pi-Durable x Extensions, Vercel Eve, Rivet, DeepSeek Agent

Environments and computers

There are two types of computers the platform needs to support: clones of checkpointed sandboxes across a variety of providers, and people's local computers. N agents should be able to work with M computers (e.g., one agent spinning up five sandboxes to experiment with different configurations, one VM per coding agent with a full environment, or 1,000 agents using 100 VMs in parallel as a swarm). These environments should be configurable agentically.

Relevant: Claude Remote, Cursor Agent, Cua AI

RBAC-ed filesystem

warms of agents will operate on a shared POSIX filesystem in the cloud, with access controls attached to the filesystem separately from the computer. This layer acts as part GitHub, where agent-generated code, extensions, and definitions live; part Google Drive, where uploaded, downloaded, and generated files and "apps" live; and more. Since it's effectively a remote shared filesystem, you could host .env files and have each directory use .git or jj for version control. There will be various configurations of RBAC that organizations will want, whether it's agents like humans, or permission granted based on who initiated the particular turn, or a mixture of both.

Relevant: Archil, S3 Filesystems, JuiceFS

Separation of session and conversation

The status quo for most coding agent applications is to expose the agent session, including its intermediate tool calls, directly to the user. I think this is wrong.

What the user interacts with should be abstracted from the core agent session as a "conversation." Your app should natively have a concept of a conversation, at the same level of abstraction as a Slack channel, iMessage chat, WhatsApp conversation, or email thread. Content intended for the user should be posted through a tool call rather than by directly exposing the assistant messages from the underlying agent session.

Direct access to agent sessions should be akin to reading the codebase: a way to inspect and debug the system, rather than the primary user interface.
ADEs created in 2025–2026 that wrap coding agent sessions (e.g., T3) will face the same kind of dilemma Cursor faced in 2025–2026. I suspect most will not survive this transition because of the innovator's dilemma.

Relevant: Duet / Grokbot / Dots

Inbox

Rather than reading through conversations, users will increasingly interact with a focused inbox of approvals and questions. The inbox should also support tenant-specific apps for reviewing intermediate work relevant to the business that requires human action.

elevant: MS Today by @nicbstme

Listeners, monitors, single-tenant data

Agents should be able to define streams of events from the external world to listen to on a per-tenant basis (WSS, Kafka streams, CDC, etc.) and translate those events, deterministically or agentically, into signals they can act on. These listeners should be buildable on the fly rather than requiring built-in support from the agent platform. This supports agents to define any form of integration to the outside world either as code or as agent. Anything from “I want my Capy Captain / Dots / Duet / main Grok Bot actually have a function for which every email comes in, have JEV filter over it, and trigger an agent run on that email” / “Nevermind, I actually want it to be batches of emails across all my accounts” / “Actually, I want emails from senders with https://t.co/wc3kCMqkQz to be handled for the next week because we need to watch for specific emails from them but I need it to be time sensitive”. Right now, the industry (Grok bot, Muse, Instinct, etc) really only supports hourly cron jobs that trigger an agent from a generalized platform perspective, and not otherwise write bespoke webhook integration as plugins into these platforms - listeners and monitors as a concept is a strict superset that supports tenants to flexibly configure the type of event-driven mechanism the actual core agent should reason over.

Relevant: Claude Code Monitor, Grokbot future feature

Workflows

Agents should be able to define durable workflows on a per-tenant basis. Many business and enterprise workflows operate over long horizons and involve a mixture of agentic and deterministic steps. The paradigm of shoddily defined drag-and-drop workflow automation (n8n, the original Zapier) is inferior to writing custom code. Given that the agent platform centralizes data flows through APIs and MCPs, it should also be the place where workflows are defined. But these should be code-defined workflows rather than drag-and-drop automations.

Relevant: Zapier Zap, Rivet Workflows

Apps

Aka Artifacts.

The status quo is that people view Replit as one category, separate from Claude Artifacts, ChatGPT Apps, or embedded widgets in ChatGPT. I think this is wrong. These all converge on the same idea of an app. All interfaces should be apps in your filesystem that users can customize. For example, the entire /conversations page should be defined as an artifact. Each user would get a "clone" of the codebase in their filesystem that can be extended or modified as needed. This parallels how an OS ships with default applications.

"Generative UI is going to come with default design components and be represented as JSON to be token-efficient!"

"No, we're going to have a separate DSL that's an HTML hybrid to be more flexible."

"No, we're going to have everything be a Rune App."

I think the answer is that the platform will simply support all of these under the concept of an App, and the specific representation won't matter as much.

The agent platform becomes the OS within which all these apps are built. At first glance, it's not obvious why we need an OS within an OS.

The core reason, and the value to the user, comes down to the customizability and extensibility of the application layer built on top of the underlying OS.

Consider how ten different accounting companies review tax forms. Every company within a vertical shares the same "noun" of "review XYZ," but the process by which each company evaluates and understands the information is bespoke. Ideally, these companies could fork Excel and create bespoke interfaces for their workloads.

This is exactly the assumption behind vertical SaaS: that companies within a vertical share enough common workflows to justify common ways of representing them. But I think this idea is broken as a venture thesis, at least in its original form. The best vertical SaaS products eventually evolve into configurable platforms, with internal or external sales engineers, consultants, and deployment teams responsible for configuring the apps for each company.

But I think this idea is broken as a venture thesis, at least in its original form. The best vertical SaaS products eventually evolve into configurable platforms, with internal or external sales engineers, consultants, and deployment teams responsible for configuring the apps for each company. Which then begs the question, why do you want a shittier platform than a generalized one where the agent can fully operate on?

My view is that this entire process will be done by agents on command, down to the most granular interface (whether you call it a single Claude Artifact or something else). Instead of relying on a vendor's implementation team to customize the software, users will be able to ask their agents to modify the applications directly. Creating these types of reverse-engineering artifacts is simply not friendly within the bounds of existing OS, but a separate application, whether on the browser or as a desktop application, has the full opportunity to support this.

T3, Claude Cowork with customization, and installable Claude Artifacts all point in this direction.

We will have different containers for apps (which themselves can also be apps):

 - Tmux-like interfaces. Already heavily explored by the better coding agent applications.

 - Apps embedded within messages. Already a default pattern, with apps in the sidebar also becoming standard in 2025–2026.

 - App-centered interfaces with chat in the sidebar. This inverts the relationship, making the app primary and chat secondary (e.g., Claude in Excel), similar to how agents are embedded in existing applications.

These types of views will all continue to exist. But we'll also have:

 - Infinite canvases (tldraw). Useful for expressing things like ComfyUI workflows or designs in tools like Paper or Figma, where an interface could be represented as an infinite canvas with each component being an image-display App.

 - Fixed canvases with layered windows. The default OS experience.

 - Resizable panels with fixed widths and heights. Similar to Metabase.

Relevant: Rex, OpenCode Rune

note_tweet.text:
Walmart started letting AI agents check out for you this week, right before Black Friday. You set a cap like $50 or $100, or make it ask before every order.

That cap is the whole lesson. Most people's AI bots don't have one.

My bots do clipping, posting, research and outreach for my business and this account. What made me trust them wasn't a smarter prompt. It was deciding what each one can do without me.

Since last week Grok Bot lets you set that per tool. Open a connected app's page and every tool gets one of 4 settings:

Always allow. It just runs.
Auto-review. A second model checks each action and only stops to ask you if something looks off.
Needs approval. It asks you every single time.
Blocked. It can't use it, even if you ask.

How I'd sort them:

Reading goes on Always allow. Search the inbox, read the calendar, open files. Nothing breaks when a bot reads.

Drafting goes on Auto-review. Email drafts, post drafts, notes.

Anything you can't take back goes on Needs approval. Emailing a customer. Deleting. Paying.

Anything that bot never needs goes on Blocked. A research bot has no reason to delete files, so why leave the door open.

The part people miss: buying stuff in Grok Bot already waits for your OK, even with a card saved in the Vault. The quiet tools are the real risk. A bot that can delete in your Drive, or email your whole contact list.

One more thing that beats every setting: write the limit into the ask. "Find it, compare, build the cart. Don't buy. Show me the total first."

If you want to try it on your Black Friday list, copy this:

"Help me with Black Friday gifts. Total budget: $___. People and their limits: ___. For each person, find 2 options under their limit from stores with free returns. Show price, store and delivery date. Don't buy anything. Wait for me to pick, then show me the full checkout total before you place any order."

A bot you'd leave alone for a weekend isn't the smartest one. It's the one with the clearest rules.

note_tweet.text:
10 tool updates you missed today 👇
The daily changelog rundown for the AI apps you actually use.

1. ChatGPT: an OpenAI engineer says a week of speed work on the desktop app makes opening a chat from cold 80% faster, switching chats 30% faster and launch 10% faster, with downloads 35% smaller on Mac and 25% on Windows. Still crawling? Probably waiting on an update.

2. GLM Coding Plan: Zhipu put GLM-5.4 live on every GLM Coding Plan today, with image understanding, and your weekly allowance goes about 50% further than on GLM-5.3. Same subscription, more runway. Rare in this business.

3. Google Chat: apps and agents can now post messages with proper tables and headings. You still can't type a table yourself, so the bots now format better than you do.

4. Google Meet: 1080p video sending on the web is now on by default for everyone, not just some paid plans, if your camera and connection can handle it. Your webcam has nowhere left to hide.

5. Claude Code: version 2.1.330 adds easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when you ask, on Pro and Max on macOS and Linux. You can turn automatic charts off in /config.

6. Claude Desktop: new recurring tasks in Code sessions, like /loop, now run for up to 30 days instead of 7. Set it, and actually forget it.

7. Meta Muse: Meta officially launched its Muse Chrome extension, which puts the agent in Chrome's side panel, working in its own tab group with your logins. Meta warns it may take unexpected actions. Read that bit twice.

8. Signal: iOS and Android updates now block screenshots by default, so Siri, Gemini and other built-in agents can't read your chats off the screen. Signal admits it's only a partial fix.

9. Grok Bot (spotted in testing, not live yet): the Mac app is getting local computer use, so a Bot could work the apps on your own desktop rather than a cloud machine, plus dictation in any app.

10. Google Antigravity (spotted in testing, not live yet): an Inbox mode listing the agent threads waiting on you, plus building an agent from a plain prompt. Less babysitting, in theory.

Every item checked against official changelogs or reputable sources. Links in the first reply.
Which of these are you actually switching on? New one every day.
